messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Two years ago, Kwame’s life fractured during a late night at a friend’s apartment. A guest he barely knew, a man he had trusted enough to share drinks with, suddenly pinned him against a hallway wall. The stranger dragged him into a study, clicked the deadbolt, and held him down while whispering crude threats about his sexual compliance. Kwame fought, but the man was heavier, faster. The only sounds were the muffled hum of the heating system and the sickening finality of the locked door. He never saw the attacker’s face clearly, only the dark fabric of his clothes and the relentless, degrading language about sexual violation that played on a loop in the confined air. When police finally arrived after neighbors called the fire department, the door was pried open, but the image of the bolted mechanism stayed seared in his mind. The specific combination of confinement, masculine aggression, and explicit sexual threats explained why those exact cues would later hijack his nervous system. In the weeks that followed, Kwame’s internal landscape shifted irrevocably. He had come to believe he was helpless to stop bad things from happening to him, and that the future held no possibility of recovery. This crushing hopelessness, paired with a fragile conviction that others could see what happened to him just by looking at him, directly amplified his physical readiness for danger. His belief that he was permanently damaged made his nervous system constantly scan for the specific cues that had once trapped him. He began avoiding any situation where he might be cornered, flinching whenever a colleague mentioned sexual violence in passing, and refusing to enter rooms that could be locked from the outside. His interpretations of his own vulnerability systematically dictated his avoidance patterns. At his private practice, this dynamic became impossible to ignore. As a psychologist, Kwame’s work required closed offices and one-on-one meetings, environments that now triggered a physiological alarm so severe he would cancel sessions rather than risk entrapment. His body’s constant state of threat monitoring dictated his avoidance patterns; the mere thought of being confined or cornered by another man caused his shoulders to stiffen and his breath to shallow. He instinctively angled his chair to face every doorway, ensuring he could see who was approaching, because he felt unsafe unless his back was against a wall where he could see the room. His hypervigilance in the clinical setting forced him to keep every door wide open, stripping his workspace of the confidentiality it was designed to protect. The more he isolated himself, the more his physical state confirmed his worst fears. Waking each night to sweat-drenched sheets because he needed to stay alert reinforced his belief that he was defenseless against sudden danger. His inability to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place meant his nervous system never recovered, which in turn made every unfamiliar sound feel like a prelude to assault. This relentless physical exhaustion validated his hopelessness, convincing him that nothing would ever change. His threat response fed his negative appraisals, and his appraisals, in turn, kept his threat system permanently armed, creating a closed loop that left him paralyzed in his own life. By his thirty-seventh month, the isolation had cost him his professional momentum and his social world. He stopped returning calls from family, his practice dwindled to virtual sessions only, and the weight of maintaining his constant vigilance left him emotionally hollow. What finally brought him to seek help was a panic attack during a telehealth session, where his hands shook so violently he could barely sign out, and a quiet realization that he was no longer living. He was hoping for a way to quiet the constant alarm in his chest, though he feared, with a familiar tightness in his throat, that he had simply lost the capacity to feel safe again. He knew the work would be uncomfortable, but staying exactly where he was was no longer an option.
